Yolanda: 'No.'
Counselor: 'Is there anything else you want to tell me?'
Yolanda: 'Well, he's outside the room with a gun.'
Counselor: 'Then how are you not in danger?'
Yolanda: 'If he was in the same room with the gun, or the gun was held to my head, then I would be in danger. He's not in the room.'
Counselor: 'Will you come back tonight?'
Yolanda: 'Yes. What time do the doors close?'

They are not lying about facts; they are refusing the conclusion.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Each statement is internally truthful about the man's surface conduct, and de Becker does not dispute that he seemed normal; that is the point, since violence is committed by people who look and act like people. But the record, three prior attempts on his wife's life and two domestic-violence arrests, was available and strongly predictive, so the neighbors' verdicts are made possible by a refusal to imagine the category 'father who kills his own children.' The pause before 'I suppose' shows the information registering while the frame resists it. The breakdown 'he must be crazy' is itself a denial device, because classifying the act as insanity averts the need to treat the warning signs as meaningful.
distractors: Conspiracy-level concealment: the neighbors are hiding knowledge of prior violence.
Exaggeration for the camera: they dramatize shock to get attention.
Accurate risk assessment: 'normal'-seeming men are empirically never killers.

assets.topic: Advocacy disguised as evidence on restraining orders
assets.visual_frame_description: A conference-hall audit view. Dr. Fenn stands at a lectern before rows of police commanders; an attendee's question is shown in a side panel along with the study fact-sheet that lists the sample as small and excluding spousal stalkers. A deflection counter lights up each time he repeats his slogan.
assets.player_mission: Audit the psychiatrist's defense of restraining orders during the Q&A and decide whether his certainty is evidence-based. Track how he handles the study's flaws versus his slogan, then enter the correct diagnosis.
key_concepts: The psychiatrist's 'proof' rested on a woefully biased study of a small sample of stalking cases that did not even include spousal stalkers, the very type most likely to kill.
Working back from the murders, restraining orders and other confrontational interventions appear alarmingly often.
The personal effects of a woman murdered by her estranged husband frequently include the restraining order.
The chemotherapy comparison is dangerously flawed because cancer cannot be gotten away from, while an estranged husband can be left.
It is dangerous to promote a specific treatment without first diagnosing the problem in the individual case.
Restraining orders are most effective on the reasonable person with limited emotional investment, the person least likely to be violent anyway.
A TRO may ask one man to do something he can easily do while asking an estranged husband to abandon the central features of his life.
The TRO hurts by convincing the woman that she is safe.
In a San Diego District Attorney's office study of 179 stalking cases, about half of the victims who had sought restraining orders felt their cases were worsened by them.
A Department of Justice study concluded that restraining orders were ineffective in stopping physical violence.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests advocacy-driven reasoning in the restraining-order debate: de Becker documents a psychiatrist citing a small, biased, non-spousal sample as proof and defending it with a flawed cancer analogy. The deflection pattern, repetition under challenge and comfort at the slogan, is the signature of a conclusion in search of evidence.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Is the psychiatrist giving an honest review of the evidence when he declares restraining orders 'proven' to work?
assets.subject_baseline: Dr. Fenn, 61, a psychiatrist and long-serving apologist for the current system, has testified for two decades in favor of uniform restraining-order recommendations. He is an articulate public speaker who cites the same small dataset in each appearance, describing it as 'the definitive study.'
observed_nonverbal_log: At the phrase 'woefully biased study, small sample' from an attendee, Dr. Fenn's blink rate rises sharply and he straightens his notes, clearing his throat twice before answering.
When the attendee specifies that the study excluded spousal stalkers, his gaze drops to the lectern and he reshuffles his papers for several seconds.
At 'some people die on chemotherapy,' he relaxes, leans on the podium, and repeats the line verbatim for the audience, smiling.
interrogation_transcript: Attendee: 'How many of the studied cases were spousal stalkers, doctor?'
Fenn: 'The relevant question is whether TROs work, and we have proven they do.'
Attendee: 'The study you cite excluded the very stalkers most likely to kill. Can you name its sample size?'
Fenn: 'Look at it this way: some people die on chemotherapy. Some people die when they get restraining orders. But that doesn't mean you don't do chemo, or that you don't get restraining orders.'
Attendee: 'Cancer cannot be avoided by leaving. This man can be left.'
Fenn: 'The paper works. We have proven it.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Advocacy-driven reasoning that obscures the evidence, not good-faith scientific reporting: Dr. Fenn cannot or will not engage the study's fatal flaw, and his chemotherapy analogy deflects rather than answers, a rhetorical maneuver that hides the fact that the woman can get away from the man while the cancer patient cannot.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The tell is structural, not just vocal: every direct question about study quality is met with either a repetition of the slogan 'TROs work, and we have proven it' or an analogy that changes the subject. De Becker reports that the psychiatrist's claim rested on a woefully biased study of a small sample of stalking cases that did not include spousal stalkers, the type most likely to kill, and that working back from the murders, restraining orders appear alarmingly often. The discomfort signs cluster exactly where the data gap sits, sample size and the excluded group, and vanish when he returns to his slogan. The chemotherapy comparison presupposes a threat the patient cannot escape, which is precisely false for a woman who can make herself unavailable to a man she can leave, and de Becker calls the comparison not only callous but dangerously flawed because the risks are not equivalent.
distractors: Honest uncertainty thoughtfully presented with appropriate caveats.
Personal testimony: his decades of clinical experience are the real evidence he is citing.
A transparent analogy that fairly compares two equivalent risks.

assets.topic: The long, slow crime at the police counter
assets.visual_frame_description: A dim police-station lobby at night. Lisa, 34, in a rumpled coat, stands at the front counter across from Sergeant Alvarez; a messy stack of intake forms rises from the cabinet behind him. The scene is rendered as a branching decision tree with the lobby, her house, and a shelter map as reachable nodes.
assets.player_mission: Assess Lisa's situation from the indicators she gives, then choose the intervention that actually protects her rather than the one that satisfies the paperwork. Confront the gap between her plan to return and the reality of her husband's escalation.
key_concepts: Lisa's husband used a gun he claimed he bought for self defense but was really for defense of the self.
The violence that preceded the final violence is in almost every case a secret kept by several people.
Being struck and forced not to resist trains out of the victim the instinctive reaction to protect the self.
The battered woman may be shell-shocked enough to believe that each horrible incident may be the last.
No amount of logic can usually move a battered woman; persuasion requires emotional leverage.
The woman who could not protect herself retained the instinct to protect her children, and it was for them that she finally left.
Shelters are where safety is, where guidance is, where wisdom is, and shelter locations are secret.
The distinction between safety and justice is blurred but real: safety requires not chasing the purse-snatcher into traffic.
Refer the woman to a battered women's shelter, if for nothing else than to speak to someone who knows about what she is facing.
Leaving is the best response to violence, but it is in trying to leave that most women get killed.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the escalation pattern of the long, slow crime and emotional-leverage persuasion: de Becker shows violence escalating by decision while the victim's fear mechanism dulls. The winning intervention makes the woman unavailable to her pursuer, because the operating goal is safety, not justice.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The long, slow crime: spousal homicide is usually the end of a sustained, escalatory pattern, not an eruption. The battle tests assembling pre-incident indicators, understanding why the victim returns, and choosing the intervention that actually increases safety rather than the one that satisfies the system.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are Sergeant Alvarez at the front desk of a night station. Lisa, 34, has climbed out a window and run through darkened streets to get here. She tells you her husband held a gun to her head tonight, that he has slapped her and choked her before, and that their children saw the gun incident. She is proud, upright, almost relieved: she plans to return home so long as he promises never to hit her again, and she expects the department to talk some sense into him. The intake sheet shows her children are seven and nine, and the address she gives is the house she fled.
assets.stage_1_question: Which reading of Lisa's situation is most accurate?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Lisa is at escalating risk, and her plan to return on a promise is the most dangerous element in the room: the violence has already escalated from slaps to choking to a gun, the children witnessed it, and his resort to a weapon places him near the center of the predictive circle for wife murder. Her calm is consistent with a dulled fear mechanism, and her expectation that the system can reform him misunderstands both him and the situation she is in.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Lisa is determined to go home tonight unless someone stops her. Four options sit on the counter: (a) hand her a temporary restraining order application and tell her to return tomorrow to file it; (b) tell her to fill out the forms, go home, and file them when she returns; (c) make the direct case that going back could be fatal and connect her to the shelter system that evening; (d) promise her that the department will bring her husband in for a talk and counsel him. Which choice is the one that actually protects her?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: (c). The sergeant who saved Lisa chose the truth: 'You fill out these forms and go back home, and the next time I look for them, it will be because you have been murdered.' De Becker's guidance is to make the woman unavailable to her pursuer and get her to people who understand that the issue is safety, not justice; shelters are where safety is, and persuasion of a battered woman requires emotional leverage, not statistics, forms, or promises that a violent man will be reformed by a conversation.

assets.topic: The restraining-order decision in an estranged-husband case
assets.visual_frame_description: A domestic-violence council office. Teresa, 39, sits across from an advocate with a protective-order packet on the desk between them; a case-file screen behind her shows Victor's record: two violated orders, six arrest warrants, a gun threat, and months of stalking. The branching interface asks whether the order helps or hurts her case.
assets.player_mission: Diagnose Teresa's case before choosing any treatment, then pick the strategy that maximizes her safety. Weigh Victor's emotional investment and entitlement against what a court order can actually accomplish, and resist the reflexive recommendation.
key_concepts: Refusing to accept rejection is more important to these men than life itself, which is why so many of these murderers also commit suicide.
Rejection is a threat to the identity, the persona, the entire self, making such crimes murder in defense of the self.
Restraining orders are most effective on the reasonable person with limited emotional investment, the person least likely to be violent anyway.
A TRO used on an estranged husband asks him to abandon the central features of his life: his relationship, his control and ownership, his identity as a powerful man and as a husband.
Many homicides have occurred at the courthouse where women were seeking protection orders, or just prior to the hearings.
Seventy-five percent of spousal murders happen after the woman leaves; estrangement, not argument, begets the worst violence.
The TRO hurts by convincing the woman that she is safe.
There is really only one good reason to get a restraining order in a case of wife abuse: the woman believes the man will honor it and leave her alone.
Shelters are where safety is; the professionals there understand that the issue is safety, not justice.
Extreme caution is urged in the period following issuance of a TRO, which is emotionally charged and hazardous.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests case diagnosis before treatment selection in the restraining-order dilemma: a TRO is only as good as the man it is used against, and for an estranged husband with deep entitlement it can escalate the violence it is meant to stop. De Becker's cases show the order working best on the people least likely to be violent anyway, and the winning move is availability-reduction, not paper.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The restraining-order dilemma: a court order is a tool whose value depends entirely on the man it is used against, and in estranged-husband cases it can provoke the violence it is meant to prevent. The battle tests diagnosing the individual case before prescribing the standard remedy.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are a domestic-violence advocate at the Los Angeles County Domestic Violence Council. Teresa, 39, estranged from her husband Victor for four months, sits opposite you. He has held a gun to her head once, stalked her for months, violated two prior orders, and told her, 'Marriage is for life and the only way out is death.' He has six active arrest warrants. Teresa has asked the court to issue a new protective order and wants your opinion on whether it will protect her. Her children are ten and twelve, and she still shares the family address with Victor, who refuses to find other housing.
assets.stage_1_question: Which assessment of Teresa's case is most accurate?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Teresa is in the highest-risk category de Becker describes: Victor is a rejecting husband with deep emotional investment and entitlement for whom a court order would demand abandoning the central features of his life, and his own words show he treats the marriage as eternal and exit as death. The order is likely to escalate rather than deter him, because restraining orders work best on the reasonable person with limited emotional investment, the person least likely to be violent anyway.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Teresa asks what she should do with the order she is about to file. Which strategic choice maximizes her safety? (a) File the order and remain at the family address, since the paper keeps police response simple; (b) file the order if she chooses, but simultaneously make herself unavailable by moving to a secret shelter location with her children and following the escape protocol of duplicate keys and documents; (c) abandon the order entirely and confront Victor directly with the divorce papers to demonstrate resolve; (d) ask the court to summon Victor at the hearing and hold him in contempt in the same session.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: (b). The order, if pursued at all, must never be treated as protection: the case history, Shirley Lowery stabbed outside the courtroom, Tammy Marie Davis killed after being served, Maria Navarro killed despite her 911 call after her order expired, shows that courthouse moments and order-serving are where these murders occur. De Becker's rule is that there is only one good reason to get a restraining order, that the woman believes the man will honor it, which Teresa has no reason to believe; safety comes from becoming unavailable, shelter locations are secret, and the family court judge's warning applies: this paper won't stop the next fist or the next bullet.
